data.description:
Goal:
A `kno sync` on 2026-08-25 in the quilt project rolled two knots BACKWARDS. Both had been driven to a later state on 2026-08-24 during a session on that workstation; after the sync they read an EARLIER state with an EARLIER updated_at than the work that had already happened.

  quilt-09be  shipped -> ready_for_implementation, updated_at 2026-08-24T09:13:13Z
  quilt-7867  shipped -> blocked,                  updated_at 2026-08-24T09:14:17Z

Both timestamps predate the session that moved them (roughly 14:00Z to 18:30Z the same day). 7867's alias also changed, 3913.23.3 -> 3913.23.4, and its notes ended with a note written before 09be shipped. The work itself is real and independently checkable in git: 7867's code merged to quilt main as 16f15fe59f42, the converge ran against four production hosts, and 7867's own commit tags SURVIVED the sync while its state did not. So the merge is not last-write-wins on the whole record: some fields took the newer stream and the state field took the older one.

That is the defect. A knot's state is the thing every dispatch, gate and report reads, and a sync that can move it backwards makes the register unable to say what has shipped. An agent reading 7867 that day would re-implement work already on main.

Fix direction: make the event merge total-ordered per knot, so a state transition can never be superseded by an event that happened before it, whatever machine it arrives from. If two streams genuinely conflict, the sync must SAY so rather than silently pick one — surface a conflict the way a land queue surfaces a rebase conflict.

Verification:
1. A knot advanced on machine A and left untouched on machine B keeps machine A's state after a sync in either direction.
2. A knot advanced on BOTH machines produces a reported conflict, not a silent winner.
3. A deterministic test drives two divergent event streams for one knot through the merge and asserts both of the above.

(Provenance: recreated from quilt-388b on 2026-08-25; the quilt copy is deferred and tracking moved here.)
